title: Metal You Can Pick Up
description: Native copper and gold, iron from the sky, and how to recognise ore in the rocks
tryIt: Visit a museum geology gallery or a rock shop, find native copper, malachite and haematite, and note how the colour of each one gives it away.

concepts.title: How it works: ready-made metal
concepts.contentHtml:
It is your first autumn. You have fire, charcoal and a few good pots, and your stone axe has just shattered on a knot of oak. There is metal in the rocks around you, but nearly all of it is locked away in ore. The easy exceptions are the metals that come ready-made.

The first metalworkers of North America smelted nothing. On the Keweenaw Peninsula of Lake Superior, the US National Park Service dates the earliest known metalworking on the continent to at least 8,000 years ago,1 when Indigenous Peoples dug shallow mines and used heavy stones to break waste rock away from masses of2 native copper, copper that occurs as pure metal. (The park's archaeology page says 7,000 years,3 so treat the date as approximate.) They hammered it into bracelets, beads, tools and fishhooks.

Native copper is soft enough to shape cold with a stone, but hammering makes it harder and more brittle, an effect called work hardening. On the Iranian plateau, the earliest copper objects turn out to be native copper that was annealed, heated between rounds of hammering, to avoid work-hardening.4 Gold is the other easy metal. It occurs in nature in its native state, and people once mined it by picking it out of streams and rivers.5 It never rusts, but it is so soft that a penny can usually scratch it:6 lovely for jewellery, useless for an axe.

The third gift falls from the sky. In 1925 Howard Carter found two daggers in the wrappings of the boy king Tutankhamun,7 one of them iron. Its blade puzzled people for decades: ironwork was rare in ancient Egypt, and the blade had not rusted. In 2016 Italian and Egyptian researchers analysed it with an X-ray fluorescence spectrometer and reported that its high nickel content, along with its levels of cobalt, strongly suggests an extraterrestrial origin.8 Its chemistry resembled a meteorite called Kharga, found at Mersa Matruh on Egypt's coast. Nine blackened iron beads from a cemetery near the Nile, dated to about 3200 BC,9 had already turned out to be hammered from meteorite iron.

concepts.title: In the field: reading rocks for ore
concepts.contentHtml:
Almost all metal hides in ore, rock in which the metal is chemically bound to oxygen, sulphur, carbon and other elements. You cannot see the metal, but you can learn the clues, and colour comes first. In the Balkans, the earliest copper smelters picked out black-and-green minerals for more than half a millennium,1 while earlier farmers there carved beads from pure green malachite.

  1. Look for green and blue. Green or blue crusts and stains on rock point to copper minerals. In Iran, smelting began in the 5th millennium BC with oxidic copper ores such as cuprite and malachite.2
  2. Look for rusty red, brown or black. These colours suggest iron oxide. Ore collected near an early iron-smelting site in Rwanda turned out to be haematite with only 1 to 2% impurities.3
  3. Check the boggy valley bottoms. Bog ore hides in wet ground. The ore for Peter Crew's smelting experiments in Wales occurs as a hard layer 15 to 20 cm thick above clay,4 where a peat-filled valley drains out, and he collected it in lumps of up to 20 kg.
  4. Look in the clay pits. In the Weald of south-east England the ore is siderite, an iron carbonate, found as buff-to-grey, bun-shaped nodules 5 to 25 cm across5 or as layers in the clay.
  5. Roast a test piece. Roasting turns Wealden ore from grey to red6 and makes it magnetic, porous and easy to crush, because the carbonate becomes oxide.7
  6. Beware of sand. Too much silica spoils an ore: with one ore of about 30% silica the Wealden group got no bloom at all, only specks of iron trapped in sticky slag.8
Safety Collect rocks only where it is legal, and keep away from old mine workings and quarry faces, which collapse. Some colourful minerals carry arsenic: weathered arsenopyrite produces green-blue scorodite,9 so green does not always mean copper. Never taste minerals, and wash your hands after handling them. Roasting has its own hazard: lumps of ore can burst from trapped steam and carbon dioxide,10 which is why the Wealden group covers its roasting pit with metal sheets.

concepts.title: Myth check: iron from the sky
concepts.contentHtml:
Meteorite iron is such a good story that it has grown legends of its own. Two are worth testing.

Myth Any ancient iron rich in nickel must come from a meteorite.
Reality Nickel is a strong clue, not proof. Iron meteorites are rich in nickel, but smelted iron can concentrate nickel too, along weld lines and in the surface layers of iron that has been repeatedly heated and forged.1 A 2019 review by Vladimir Zavyalov and Nataliya Terekhova notes that nickel enrichment of 4 to 10% in such layers is not exceptional,2 and concludes that chemical composition alone cannot be used as unambiguous evidence of a meteoritic origin;3 you also need to look at the metal's structure under a microscope.4 The famous Ugarit axe from Syria, made around 1450–1350 BC, shows how hard this is: it has been argued to be both smelted and meteoritic, and its origin is still disputed.5
Myth Meteorite iron taught people how to make iron.
Reality The dates do not line up neatly. In Eastern Europe, meteorite-iron objects appear in the 3rd millennium BC, while smelted iron turns up only around the end of the 2nd and the start of the 1st millennium BC,6 as smelting knowledge spread from Anatolia. Smelting grew out of fire and ore, not the sky. The same review even suggests the arrow may have pointed the other way: once smiths had learned to smelt and forge iron, they got better at working the meteorite kind.7

Wait, really? The Egyptians seem to have known where their rare iron came from. The researchers who studied Tutankhamun's dagger point out that around the 13th century BC a term literally translated as "iron of the sky" came into use to describe all types of iron.8

title: Copper and Bronze
description: Smelting green rocks with charcoal, why tin hardens copper, and the Bronze Age tin trade
tryIt: Find a bronze statue, plaque or bell near you and look for the green crust where rain runs off it: the same colour family as the malachite that early smelters hunted.

concepts.title: How it works: the first smelt
concepts.contentHtml:
Picture a pit dug into the ground and lined with broken pots, packed with glowing charcoal and a few crumbly black-and-green stones. Hours later you rake through the ashes and find tiny beads of red metal in a glassy crust. You have just repeated an experiment from 7,000 years ago.

The oldest firm evidence of smelting, getting metal out of ore with heat, comes from Belovode, a Vinča culture village in Serbia. About 5 g of copper slag found there, dated to around 5000 BC, is the earliest recorded copper production in Eurasia,1 according to a study by the archaeometallurgist M. Radivojević. Fragments of pottery with slag stuck to them were probably pieces that lined a hole in the ground,2 so the first furnaces may have been little more than lined pits.

Smelting is a tug of war over oxygen. In the ore, copper is chemically bonded to oxygen and other elements. Burning charcoal gives off carbon monoxide, a gas that grabs oxygen; inside the fire it pulls oxygen off the ore and leaves metal behind.3 Chemists call this reduction, and a fire that does it is a reducing one. The Belovode slags point to a gas atmosphere that was slightly oxidising to moderately reducing,4 which was enough to make copper.

How hot? Droplets of copper trapped in the Balkan slags had melted completely, which shows the fires reached about 1083 °C.5 The smelters' favourite rocks may have helped: manganese oxides in those black-and-green minerals made the ore easier to reduce in a fire that was hard to control.6

concepts.title: In the field: how Bronze Age smiths made bronze
concepts.contentHtml:
Pure copper is soft and awkward to cast. Add tin and you get bronze. A review of ancient Iranian metallurgy by Omid Oudbashi and colleagues sums up why it mattered: tin helps copper flow and cast, and with about 10% tin the metal is harder and stronger than copper alloyed with arsenic or zinc.1 Tin also lowers copper's melting point.2 This is history, not a recipe, but here is how Bronze Age smiths got the job done.

  1. Win the copper. Smelt copper ore, as in the last concept, and gather the metal.
  2. Find tin, or someone who sells it. Where Bronze Age tin came from is still one of the great mysteries of prehistoric archaeology, and some of the best-known tin ingots come from shipwrecks.
  3. Get the proportions right. About one part tin to nine or ten of copper. The Uluburun ship, wrecked off Turkey shortly before 1320 BC,3 carried 10 tons of copper ingots and one ton of tin, most likely meant to be alloyed together.
  4. Alloy under charcoal. One ancient method added tin ore, cassiterite, to molten copper in a crucible under a cover of charcoal, at about 1200 °C.4 The charcoal keeps conditions reducing,5 so the tin is freed from its ore straight into the copper.
  5. Cast it. Pour the runny bronze into a mould.
  6. Finish the edge. Cold hammering work-hardens the cutting edge, and annealing softens the metal again if it needs more shaping.
Safety Molten bronze is hotter than 1000 °C, and melting it is a job for a properly equipped, supervised workshop. Water is the hidden enemy: the UK Health and Safety Executive warns that water contamination of any molten metal can cause explosions, often from wet scrap.6 Some old copper ores and alloys contain arsenic, and fumes from hot metal can make you ill. Never melt metal indoors or on your own.

concepts.title: Myth check: who invented bronze, and whose tin?
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Bronze was a recipe some genius sat down and invented.
Reality The first alloys were probably happy accidents, because many copper ores carry other metals with them. On the Iranian plateau, early metalworkers who melted native copper containing arsenic minerals made1 arsenical copper without meaning to, and alloys of copper and arsenic spread across the Near East in the second half of the 4th millennium BC.2 In the Balkans, the earliest tin bronzes are linked to colourful ores that naturally contained both copper and tin.3 Smiths noticed the golden colour, the hardness and the easier casting,4 and deliberate recipes followed: a copper-arsenic alloy made on purpose was often a stepping stone between plain cast copper and tin bronze.5
Myth Everyone knows Bronze Age tin came from Cornwall.
Reality Cornwall is a candidate, but nobody can yet prove where the Uluburun tin came from. In 2022 a team led by Powell argued from scientific data and archaeological evidence that it came partly from Central Asia, around the Mushiston deposit, and partly from Anatolia, at Kestel and Hisarcık.6 In 2023 Daniel Berger and colleagues replied that Mushiston is not a source, that tin deposits in Cornwall, the Erzgebirge and Iberia have similar tin isotopes,7 and that no definite statements can yet be made about the origin of the tin.8

Wait, really? Tin makes a slippery witness. Tin objects are extremely rare finds, and the metal itself can fall apart: below about 13 °C the crystal structure of tin can change, turning the white metal into a grey powder.

title: Iron from the Bloomery
description: Why iron needs a hotter, reducing furnace, what slag does, and hammering a spongy bloom
tryIt: Leave a pad of plain steel wool damp in a jar for a week and watch it rust: that red-brown iron oxide is the reaction a bloomery runs backwards.

concepts.title: How it works: iron that never melts
concepts.contentHtml:
Copper was the warm-up. Iron ore is everywhere, in bogs, clay pits and red rocks, yet iron tools arrived thousands of years after copper ones. The reason is heat.

Pure iron melts at about 1540 °C, far hotter than an ancient charcoal furnace could reach.1 So for most of the last three thousand years, as Paul Craddock and J. Lang explain, iron was made by the bloomery process, entirely in the solid state.2 Instead of a pool of molten metal, the furnace yields a bloom: a spongy lump of iron riddled with glassy waste, some of which stays trapped in the finished metal as threads of slag.3

The chemistry is reduction again, run harder. Experiments by the Wealden Iron Research Group show that charcoal can in theory start reducing iron ore above about 680 °C, but only reaches a useful rate above about 900 °C.4 Carbon monoxide from the burning charcoal rises through the furnace, stripping oxygen from the ore, and the rate of reduction increases as the ore sinks towards the hottest zone in front of the air pipe,5 the tuyère.

Now the clever part. The iron never melts, but much of the iron in the ore combines with the sand and clay in it to form a molten6 slag, which carries particles of solid iron down through the furnace until they clump together.7 Craddock and his colleagues explain why this matters: the tiny iron particles form inside the slag, which protects them from oxidising again, so a liquid slag is essential.8 The furnace must also stay reducing: the Wealden smelters finish every smelt with a last charge of charcoal alone,9 to keep conditions reducing while the final ore works its way down.

concepts.title: In the field: running a bloomery
concepts.contentHtml:
A bloomery is a clay chimney. The Wealden Iron Research Group's experimental furnace, believed similar in design to Roman ones,1 is about one metre high, with walls 26 cm thick around a shaft 30 cm across,2 a slag-tapping arch at the bottom and an air pipe. It is an all-day job for a trained team, not a garden project: Peter Crew found that one smelter-smith and two bellows workers was the minimum crew.3

  1. Prepare the ore. Roast it, then break it to about 10 mm; break the charcoal to about 20 mm4 and sieve out the dust so the gases can pass.
  2. Preheat. Warm the furnace overnight with a wood fire, then fill it with charcoal and blow hard.
  3. Burn off the gas. Carbon monoxide pours out of the top, so the group sets it alight to stop the toxic gas escaping.5
  4. Charge. When the top reaches about 750–800 °C, add ore and charcoal6 every 10 to 15 minutes to keep the furnace full. Crew found that equal weights of each may be the best ratio for bog ore.7
  5. Blow steadily. Keep the bellows going. Around 1050 °C at the lower temperature probe is typical, though anything from 950 to 1125 °C has produced blooms.8
  6. Tap the slag. After about three hours, open the arch9 and let the molten slag run out before it chokes the air pipe.
  7. Pull the bloom. After about five hours and 15 to 20 kg each of ore and charcoal, break the bloom off the wall with a crowbar. From 15 kg of ore the group typically gets a bloom of 1.5 kg.10
Safety Carbon monoxide is the silent danger of every furnace and forge. The NHS warns that it is colourless and does not smell,11 and lists headache, dizziness, feeling sick, weakness, confusion and shortness of breath among the symptoms. Smelters work outdoors and connect the bellows with a long hose, so the pumpers stay far enough from the furnace not to breathe the gas.12 Molten slag causes deep burns. To see a smelt, join an experimental archaeology event; do not try it alone.

concepts.title: Myth check: smelting is not melting
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Smelting iron means melting it out of the rock.
Reality In a bloomery the iron stays solid from start to finish; only the slag melts. Smelters even have to stop the iron soaking up too much carbon, because its melting point decreases as its carbon content increases:1 cast iron with 4.3% carbon melts at 1130 °C, a temperature easily exceeded in a bloomery, while pure iron needs 1550 °C2 by the Wealden group's figure (Craddock and Lang say about 1540 °C; sources round differently). A bloom usually holds no more than 0.8% carbon.3
Myth The bloom comes out of the furnace as a bar of iron, ready to use.
Reality A bloom is a spongy, slag-filled lump. In Peter Crew's experiments in Wales, the first stage of smithing alone took 2.5 hours and 24 heats.4 At first only a few hammer blows could be struck on each heat, otherwise the bloom shattered.5 The result was a billet of 880 grams, just 21% of the iron in the ore.6 With further losses, he estimated that only about 8% of the iron ends up in a finished object.7

Wait, really? Crew worked out the full bill. One kilogram of fully smithed bar iron, made from bog ore in a low shaft furnace, needed about 100 kg of charcoal and about 25 days of one person's work,8 counting the ore, the charcoal-making, the smelt and the smithing. Iron ore is cheap; iron is not.

title: At the Forge: Iron into Steel
description: Carbon and steel, reading heat colours, welding, quenching, tempering and the folding myth
tryIt: Watch a blacksmith demonstration at a heritage site or craft fair, note the colour of the iron each time it comes out of the fire, and match it to the heat chart in this lesson.

concepts.title: How it works: a pinch of carbon
concepts.contentHtml:
Your bloom is now a bar. Bend it and it bends; strike a stone with it and the edge folds over. It makes a fine hinge, but a chisel made from it would be useless. The difference between soft iron and a tool that holds an edge is a pinch of carbon.

Iron and steel are mostly the same element; what changes is the carbon. Robert Harcourt's 1917 forging textbook puts common wrought iron at about 0.04% carbon,1 mild steel at about 0.05 to 0.5%,2 and high-carbon tool steel at 0.5 to 1.6%.3 Above about 2% carbon you have cast iron, which melts low enough to pour. Harcourt's rule of thumb still holds: increasing the carbon increases strength and hardening power, but decreases ductility and weldability.4

A bloom is patchy. Inside, the Wealden group finds anything from almost no carbon to 0.5%, and occasionally 0.8% at the surface.5 Parts with more than about 0.3% carbon behave like engineering steel and can be hardened by quenching from about 850 °C,6 while the near-carbon-free parts stay soft and easy to forge.

Why does quenching harden steel? Above 727 °C, steel turns into a high-temperature form called austenite. Cool it slowly and it becomes pearlite, fine layers of soft iron (ferrite) and iron carbide (cementite). Cool it suddenly, by quenching in water, and you get needle-shaped martensite. A 2025 study of ancient Greek steel tools puts it plainly: martensite is the hardest form of iron-carbon alloy, but it is brittle.

concepts.title: In the field: what a smith actually does
concepts.contentHtml:
Forging is mostly heat management, and before thermometers smiths read heat by colour. Edward Markham's 1913 steel manual gives a table for full daylight running from dark red at about 700 °C, through cherry at about 900 °C and orange at about 1100 °C,1 to white at about 1300 °C2 (converted from his Fahrenheit figures). Light changes everything, so old manuals tell you to judge a cooling tool by holding it in a dark place.3

  1. Choose your fuel. Markham ranks them: coke is better than coal, and charcoal is better than coke.4
  2. Draw out and upset. Hammering a hot bar on the anvil makes it longer and thinner (drawing out); striking its hot end against the anvil makes it shorter and fatter (upsetting). Smiths upset the ends before a weld to allow for iron lost to scale.5
  3. Forge-weld. Bring two pieces to welding heat, when the iron looks almost white. Just before it gets there, explosive sparks fly out of the fire.6 Powdered borax lowers the melting point of the scale so the pieces can join.7 Pull the bar out promptly: burned iron is useless.
  4. Harden. Heat a high-carbon steel tool to a dull or cherry red and plunge it into water.8 It comes out very hard, and brittle.9
  5. Temper. Polish the hardened part and reheat it gently, watching coloured oxide films creep along: pale yellow at about 220 °C, then straw, brown and purple, to blue at about 290 °C.10 The lower the temperature, the less hardness you lose.11 Then cool it.
Safety Learn to forge on a course or at a club forge before building your own. Charcoal and coal fires make carbon monoxide, so never run a forge in a shed or garage: the NHS warns that barbecues used indoors and engines run in enclosed spaces cause dangerous build-ups.12 Never heat galvanised (zinc-coated) steel;13 its fumes cause metal fume fever, with chills, fever and cough. Wear eye protection, cotton or wool clothes and leather boots, and remember that iron too cool to glow can still burn you badly.

concepts.title: Myth check: folded a thousand times
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth The finest blades were folded thousands of times, and every fold made them stronger.
Reality Folding is real; the numbers are not. Each fold doubles the layers, so twenty folds already make over a million. In traditional Japanese sword-making, fragments of the bloom steel, tamahagane, were forged into small plates, welded together, then bent and welded again many times, maybe 20 to 301 according to the metallurgist Jerzy Piaskowski. The point was not magic but turning patchy raw steel into something usable: the bloom ranged from almost no carbon to about 1.5%.2 Piaskowski found far fewer slag inclusions in the core of the sword he examined than in its edge,3 and suggested that repeated folding may have been used only on the soft, low-carbon steel of the core.
Myth Steel is at its best straight out of the quench.
Reality Fresh from the water it is at its most brittle. Markham's manual is blunt: tempering high-carbon steel is for reducing the brittleness produced by hardening.4 A study of Archaic Greek tools from Miletus found that quenching was most commonly followed by tempering, holding the object at moderate temperatures to mitigate brittleness, in some cases at around 200 °C.

Wait, really? Japanese smiths quenched a blade once and got two steels. They coated the back with a thick layer of clay5 and the edge with only a very thin one. In the sword Piaskowski examined, the fast-cooled edge had turned to martensite with a hardness of about 800 kg/mm²,6 while the clay-covered back stayed soft and tough.

title: Casting and Recycling
description: Lost-wax casting, scrap as your richest ore, and the Damascus and single-invention myths
tryIt: Make a small figure from modelling wax or a candle stub, coat it thickly in plaster or air-drying clay, and notice that the only way to get a shape with undercuts out of its mould would be to melt it: the idea behind lost-wax casting.

concepts.title: How it works: lost-wax casting
concepts.contentHtml:
You need a bell, a buckle, a little gear wheel with curved spokes. You could carve each one out of solid metal, or make it once in wax and let fire do the rest.

That is lost-wax casting, one of the great inventions of the ancient world, and investment casting based on it is still important today.1 A. Garbacz-Klempka and colleagues, who studied a Bronze Age casting workshop in Poland, describe the basic method: shape a model in wax, cover it in clay and let it dry, melt the wax out, fire the mould, then pour in the metal.2 Clay moulds were generally broken up after pouring,3 so each mould makes one casting. For hollow castings, a clay core sits inside the wax.4

The oldest known lost-wax casting is a small wheel-shaped amulet about 6,000 years old from Mehrgarh in Baluchistan, Pakistan.5 M. Thoury and colleagues explain how we know: the amulet's ring and spokes make undercuts, so it could not have been pulled out of a rigid mould without breaking it.6 Only a wax model, melted away, could have made it. The metal was very pure copper, possibly native copper, melted in air above 1,085 °C.7 By about 2500 BC the method was also in use in Mesopotamia.8

concepts.title: In the field: scrap is your best ore
concepts.contentHtml:
In a rebuilt world your richest mine is the scrap heap. Metal, unlike stone, can in theory be recycled for ever,1 as a team led by Ruiliang Liu put it in a study of Bronze Age China, and Bronze Age people made the most of it: the rise of the Scandinavian Bronze Age partly depended on recycling imported objects.2 At the Late Bronze Age mining site of Prigglitz in Austria, imported copper alloys were mixed and recycled with locally smelted copper.

  1. Sort by spark. Touch a piece of iron or steel to a turning grindstone: the more carbon, the brighter the sparks.3 Wrought iron throws light-straw sparks in straight lines;4 high-carbon steel throws white sparks that burst far more often.5
  2. Reject zinc. Galvanised (zinc-coated) steel gives off zinc oxide fumes when heated, and metal fume fever was first described among brass founders.6
  3. Keep scrap dry. The HSE names wet scrap as one of the commonest causes of molten-metal explosions:7 store it under cover, dry and check it, and punch holes in any drums so liquid can drain out.8
  4. Weld iron, do not melt it. Iron goes back to the forge, not a crucible. In a faggot weld, small pieces of scrap such as old horseshoes, bolts and nuts are piled together, bound with wire, brought to welding heat and hammered into one solid lump.
  5. Melt the copper alloys. Bronze and copper can be remelted and recast, as the casting cakes, drops and sprue found at Prigglitz show.
  6. Save the hammer scale. The flakes that fly off the anvil are pure iron oxide.9 The Wealden group adds them back into the smelt, and suspects Roman smelters did the same.10
Safety Melting and casting metal is the most dangerous job in this course and belongs in a supervised foundry class. Dry every mould, tool and piece of scrap before it goes near molten metal. Wear a face shield, leather gloves, leather boots and natural-fibre clothes, never cast alone, and never melt metal indoors: the fire makes carbon monoxide, and zinc-bearing metals give off fumes that cause metal fume fever.

concepts.title: Myth check: Damascus and the one-time invention
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Damascus steel was made by folding the metal thousands of times.
Reality The famous watered-pattern Damascus blades of India and the Islamic world are generally believed to have been forged from1 wootz, a crucible steel from India, not folded. Wootz was made by stacking closed crucibles of low-carbon iron in a large furnace and firing them for 14 to 24 hours at up to 1200 °C in a strongly reducing atmosphere.2 Damascus swords have a very high carbon content of about 1.5 to 2.0%,3 and metallurgists have long tried to explain their wavy pattern through the crystal structure of the wootz ingot itself.4 The earliest surviving Damascus-patterned steels date from the 13th and 14th centuries AD.5
Myth Iron was invented once, in one place, and spread from there.
Reality That is an open argument. Iron smelting is attested in both West and East Africa from at least the first part of the 1st millennium BC,6 in slag-pit furnaces that Paul Craddock and colleagues call a purely local innovation,7 with nothing like them in the Mediterranean or the Near East. They write that the possibility of an independent invention cannot be easily dismissed.8 Yet they also give the case against: a bloomery depends on a liquid slag, and that skill seems to have grown out of the slag-making copper smelting of the Near East from the 3rd millennium BC,9 which has no early counterpart south of the Sahara. Radiocarbon dates for some early African smelting sites have caused problems too.10

Wait, really? Traditional iron smelting carried on in many parts of Africa until the recent past.11 Some furnaces were recorded while still working, and elsewhere former smelters have taken part in rebuilding and rerunning them.
